edges.description: The abnormal fetal epidermis sheds corneocytes into the amniotic fluid, producing echogenic sediment visible on ultrasound. Why the defective epidermis sheds so much material in utero has not been studied directly.

The proposed route from the skin defect to eosinophilia, raised IgE and allergy is epicutaneous sensitization through the defective barrier. This is one of the explanations the literature offers, not a demonstrated one.
The newborn skin is red and swollen beneath the scale, which regresses as the scale sheds.
After the neonatal period a mild, nonscaly ichthyosis persists, the residual expression of the barrier defect.
The hyperkeratotic fetal epidermis is the thick, greasy, vernix-like scale seen at delivery.

nodes.description: The fetal and neonatal stratum corneum fails as a permeability barrier. In the mouse this is lethal shortly after birth; in humans the barrier defect is most severe in fetal and neonatal skin and is partly compensated later. Restoring FATP4 with an intact acyl-CoA synthetase domain in suprabasal keratinocytes alone rescues the mouse skin phenotype, placing the defect in the epidermis rather than in a systemic or placental lipid disturbance.
